newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia 97/98 wool production seen up three pct.
newsitem.headline: Australia 97/98 wool production seen up three pct.

text.p: Australian wool production is forecast to increase by almost three percent in 1997/98 (June 30) to end a seven-year downward trend, Wesfarmers Dalgety Ltd said in its Wool Supply Outlook released on Monday.

A survey of wool growers conducted by Wesfarmers Dalgety in April revealed that production in all states in 1997/98 was expected to be higher than in The current season, Wesfarmers Dalgety research and information manager Judy Barraclough said.
The prediction was based on expectations of better seasonal conditions and a slowdown in the rate at which producers were shifting into cropping and away from wool production, she said.
"The survey indicates that in 1997/98 sheep numbers will increase by almost two percent, mainly reflecting improved lambing percentages," she said.
The forecast percentage changes for 1997/98 indicate that wool production will increase to about 665 million kg from 647 million kg in the current season.
Shorn sheep numbers will be around 148 million head, up from an estimated 146 million, she said.

The most dramatic turnaround in wool production trends was expected in Queensland. After about five years of drought in most areas of the state, seasonal conditions improved markedly last year in southern Queensland and early this year in the northern wool growing areas, Barraclough said.

As a result, survey participants in Queensland expected average cut per head would significantly increase and predict that wool production will be around 11 percent higher in 1997/98, she said. Growers plan to rebuild flock numbers.
In the largest wool producing state, New South Wales, production volumes and shorn sheep numbers are expected to increase by almost three percent in 1997/98.
Seasonal conditions have improved during the current season after last year's drought. Sheep productivity and the volume of woool produced has therefore increased, Barraclough said.

Victorian wool producers in the survey predicted wool production would be around three percent higher in 1997/98 compared with the current season, largely because of expectations of increased cut per head, she said.
However, deteriorating seasonal conditions at the time of the survey may have an unanticipated negative impact on the productivity of sheep in Victoria, she said.

"One of the significant features of the last two years has been the trend for growers to hold part of their clip. The Wesfarmers Dalgety survey results indicate that between 20 percent and 40 percwent of all wool producers are holding some wool in brokers' stores or on farm," she said.
Although still historically high, the proportion had reduced since the 1996 survey when about half of the survey participants were storing wool.

The greatest incidence of this was in the mixed farming areas where income from cropping had allowed growers to withhold their wool from the market in anticipation of better prices in the future, Barraclough said.
The Wool Supply Outlook is based on a random sample of 684 growers from across Australia.
The results of the survey are consistent with the previous survey undertaken in April 1996, she added.
